description: We’re APOAPSIS, a virtual team of three driven by AI, software development, science, and space exploration. Our mission is to turn NASA’s open data into innovative solutions to real world challenges through creative thinking, technical execution, and collaboration.
summary: Outpost Zero is a short browser game that helps students feel how power, water, oxygen, food, and radiation protection compete for the same limited reserves in a lunar outpost.
details: Project description Outpost Zero puts the player in charge of a fictional lunar south polar outpost for five cycles. Each cycle the player commits one action out of six: service the solar arrays, thicken the regolith shelter, service the water processor, overhaul the oxygen generator, run a greenhouse cycle, or ration the crew's food. Every action spends stored reserves, and then the cycle settles power generation, upkeep, and any scripted event. The consequence report is the heart of the game. It shows the value of each system before and after the cycle, then breaks the change into ordered steps: the action's own effect, the power balance, crew upkeep, and the event. A short explanation says why the trade off happened, and a labelled source note ties it to NASA material. A solar particle event before cycle 2 and a dust deposit on the array before cycle 4 make the same lesson concrete: protection and maintenance are cheaper before the problem arrives. After five cycles the mission ends as secured, at risk, or failed, and the debrief shows final values, the objectives met or missed, the costliest choice, and two takeaways with their sources. Students can replay immediately and compare runs, because events are deterministic. Challenge response The challenge asks for a trainer that lets students run a lunar or Martian outpost and balance the systems that keep a crew alive. Outpost Zero does that in a form a first time player can finish in a few minutes: All five systems in the challenge are playable: power, water, oxygen, food, and radiation protection, with crew condition as the outcome that the others protect. The decisions genuinely compete. The greenhouse lifts food by 18 FU while spending 11 PU and 7 WU, so feeding the crew costs the systems that keep them breathing. Servicing the array costs 8 PU now for 5 PU more generation in every later cycle, which only pays back if enough cycles remain. The learning is visible, not implied. Each result is explained in the same order every turn, so a teacher can pause on any line and ask why. The science is traceable. Every science note carries a NASA fact, data derived, or game assumption label and links to the source entry, including its limitation. Failure is a lesson, not a dead end. Emptying a reserve ends the mission early with an explanation of what ran out and which actions spent it. What is innovative or useful Most resource games show bars that go up and down. Outpost Zero explains the mechanism: the same reserve that buys an improvement is the reserve that keeps the crew alive, and the report decomposes every number into an ordered cause. That makes the trade off discussable in a classroom instead of merely felt, and it gives a teacher a concrete follow up question after each cycle: what would you protect first if you played again? AI tools used ChatGPT and Codex CLI helped plan and specify; an OpenCode agent running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free implemented and tested the application and prepared the video from real gameplay. The team owns the rules, the review, the source checks, and the submission. Full details are in the repository file AI_TOOLS_LOG.md.
